lead: Design converts the ripple formulas into hardware: core, turns, air gap, wire and capacitor. The converter chapter gives L and C; design fixes peak current, peak flux, current density and temperature rise so nothing saturates or burns. Every phone charger is this step. Done right, the converter meets ripple at 90 % efficiency; done wrong, the inductor saturates on the first overload.
prereq: You need: Chapter 3.3 and Chapter 3.4 for L, C and ripple current, Chapter 3.7 for skin effect and high-frequency loss, and Unit 1, Switching losses, thermal design and heat sinks, for thermal resistance.

sections.h3: Inductor: peak current, turns and air gap

blocks.text: The inductor starts from L, the average current I<sub>avg</sub> and the peak-to-peak ripple ΔI<sub>L</sub>. The core must carry the peak, not the average. Sizing on the average lets the core saturate every switching cycle.

blocks.where: I<sub>pk</sub> is the peak winding current in A; I<sub>avg</sub> the average current in A; ΔI<sub>L</sub> the peak-to-peak ripple in A.

N is the number of turns; L the inductance in H; I<sub>pk</sub> the peak current in A; B<sub>max</sub> the allowed peak flux density in T (about 0.3 T for ferrite); A<sub>e</sub> the effective core area in m² from the datasheet.

blocks.text: Round N up to a whole number, then recompute B = L·I<sub>pk</sub>/(N·A<sub>e</sub>) to confirm B stays below B<sub>max</sub>. Fewer turns means more flux.

blocks.where: ℓ<sub>g</sub> is the total air-gap length in m (valid when the gap dominates core reluctance); µ<sub>0</sub> = 4π × 10<sup>−7</sup> H/m; N the turns; A<sub>e</sub> in m²; L in H.

blocks.text: Most energy sits in the air gap, so the gap sets both L and the saturation current. An ungapped ferrite core cannot give both the required L and a useful saturation current: turns needed for L make I<sub>sat</sub> small; cutting turns to raise I<sub>sat</sub> drops L.

Wire comes from a current density J of 2 to 4 A/mm²: copper area Acu = Irms/J, where Irms is the RMS winding current. At 100 kHz the skin depth in copper is about 0.21 mm, so use strands under about 0.4 mm, or litz wire (Chapter 3.7). Thicker strands waste copper: current crowds to the surface and AC resistance climbs.

sections.h3: Transformer: turns ratio and window area

blocks.text: The turns ratio comes first, from the gain formula. A forward converter gives V<sub>o</sub> = D · V<sub>s</sub> · N<sub>s</sub>/N<sub>p</sub>, so the duty cycle at nominal input fixes the ratio. In a flyback the ratio sets the reflected voltage and the leakage-inductance spike.

The window must hold both windings. With fill factor k<sub>u</sub> about 0.4, N<sub>p</sub>A<sub>p</sub> + N<sub>s</sub>A<sub>s</sub> ≤ k<sub>u</sub>A<sub>w</sub>, where A<sub>p</sub> and A<sub>s</sub> are bare copper areas and A<sub>w</sub> the window area from the datasheet. If it does not fit, take a bigger core, not thinner wire that overheats.
Core loss grows with frequency and flux swing ΔB. About 0.3 T is the ferrite saturation ceiling. At 100 kHz the loss curve sets the working flux: often a peak of 0.10 to 0.15 T, not saturation.
A flyback transformer is a gapped inductor that also isolates, so the gap rule applies. A forward transformer must reset its core every cycle.
Capacitance comes from the converter ripple formula, but output ripple has two parts: charge on C and drop across equivalent series resistance (ESR).

blocks.where: ΔV<sub>o</sub> is output ripple in V; ΔI<sub>L</sub> inductor ripple in A; ESR in Ω; f<sub>s</sub> switching frequency in Hz; C in F. The 8 holds for a buck converter in continuous conduction.

blocks.text: At 100 kHz with an electrolytic, ESR usually dominates: a 100 µF part with 100 mΩ ESR gives more ripple than the capacitance term. Choose C for the capacitance term, then check ESR ≤ (ΔV<sub>o</sub> − capacitive part)/ΔI<sub>L</sub>.

Two more checks. RMS ripple current through the capacitor is about ΔI<sub>L</sub>/√12 and must stay under the datasheet rating; electrolytic life halves for every 10 °C rise. Ceramic parts have low ESR and suit high frequency, but capacitance falls under DC bias, so read the value at working voltage.

Add copper loss I<sub>rms</sub>²R<sub>ac</sub> (R<sub>ac</sub> is above R<sub>dc</sub> because of skin and proximity effect) to core loss from the curve. Multiply total by thermal resistance R<sub>th</sub> from the datasheet: ΔT = P<sub>total</sub> · R<sub>th</sub>. Keep the winding below its insulation class limit with margin for a hot Indian summer inside a sealed box.

figure.caption: N = 15.3 rounds up to 16 turns, bringing the flux down to 0.29 T; the 0.32 mm gap sets the saturation current.

spec.aria: A top-to-bottom flow from the specified L, average current and ripple through peak current 4.6 A, core area and flux limit, 16 turns, a 0.32 mm gap with 0.29 T, a 1.0 mm² wire, to the loss and temperature check.

examples.question: Design the inductor for the buck converter of Chapter 3.3: V<sub>s</sub> = 50 V, V<sub>o</sub> = 20 V, I<sub>o</sub> = 4 A, f<sub>s</sub> = 100 kHz, L = 100 µH, ripple ΔI<sub>L</sub> = 1.2 A. The core has A<sub>e</sub> = 1.0 cm² = 1.0 × 10<sup>−4</sup> m² and B<sub>max</sub> = 0.3 T. (a) Peak current. (b) Turns and resulting flux. (c) Air gap. (d) Copper area and wire diameter for J = 4 A/mm².
steps: Peak current: I<sub>pk</sub> = I<sub>o</sub> + ΔI<sub>L</sub>/2 = 4 + 0.6 = 4.6 A. The core must carry 4.6 A, not 4 A.
Round up to 16 turns. Check: B = 4.6 × 10<sup>−4</sup>/(16 × 1.0 × 10<sup>−4</sup>) = 0.2875 ≈ 0.29 T, below 0.3 T.
Copper area: A<sub>cu</sub> = I<sub>o</sub>/J = 4 A / 4 A/mm² = 1.0 mm².

Single-wire diameter: d = √(4A/π) = √(4 × 1.0/π) = 1.13 ≈ 1.1 mm, above twice the 0.21 mm skin depth. Use about eight strands of 0.40 mm (8 × π/4 × 0.40² = 1.0 mm²), or litz wire of the same copper area.
examples.answer: I<sub>pk</sub> = 4.6 A; 16 turns give B = 0.29 T; gap 0.32 mm; copper area 1.0 mm² (1.1 mm single wire, split into strands under 0.4 mm for 100 kHz).
examples.check:
import math
Vs=50.0; Vo=20.0; Io=4.0; fs=100e3; L=100e-6; ripple=1.2
Ae=1.0e-4; Bmax=0.3; J=4.0
mu0=4*math.pi*1e-7
Ipk=Io+ripple/2
print(f"{Ipk:.1f}")
N=L*Ipk/(Bmax*Ae)
print(f"{N:.1f}")
Nt=16
B=L*Ipk/(Nt*Ae)
print(f"{B:.2f}")
lg=mu0*Nt**2*Ae/L
print(f"{lg*1e3:.2f}")
Acu=Io/J
print(f"{Acu:.1f}")
d=math.sqrt(4*Acu/math.pi)
print(f"{d:.1f}")

traps: Sizing the core on average current instead of peak. The core saturates at the top of every ripple, inductance collapses and switch current spikes.
Choosing C from ΔI<sub>L</sub>/(8f<sub>s</sub>C) alone. Ripple is usually set by ESR × ΔI<sub>L</sub>, so the part meets the value on paper and fails on the bench.
Forgetting that the air gap stores energy. An ungapped ferrite core has high inductance but saturates at small current, so the design works at no load and fails at full load.
Using DC resistance for loss at 100 kHz. Skin and proximity effect can make R<sub>ac</sub> several times R<sub>dc</sub>, so the winding runs hotter than calculated.
Mixing units: A<sub>e</sub> in cm² (1 cm² = 1 × 10<sup>−4</sup> m²) and L in µH. Convert both to m² and H before dividing.

quiz.q: What peak flux density is normally allowed in a ferrite core, and which current sets the turns?
quiz.a: About 0.3 T. The peak current I<sub>pk</sub> = I<sub>avg</sub> + ΔI<sub>L</sub>/2 sets the turns, not the average.

quiz.q: Why is an air gap deliberately cut in a buck-converter inductor?
quiz.a: The gap stores most magnetic energy and adds reluctance, so the core needs more turns for the same L and saturates at a much higher current. The gap fixes both L and saturation current.

quiz.q: An inductor carries 5 A average with 2 A peak-to-peak ripple. L = 200 µH, A<sub>e</sub> = 2 cm², B<sub>max</sub> = 0.3 T. Find the number of turns.
The output ripple must be 50 mV and ΔI<sub>L</sub> = 1.2 A at f<sub>s</sub> = 100 kHz. With C = 100 µF, show whether capacitance alone meets the spec and find the maximum ESR.
quiz.a: Capacitive part = 1.2/(8 × 100 × 10³ × 100 × 10<sup>−6</sup>) = 15 mV. That leaves 35 mV for ESR, so ESR ≤ 0.035/1.2 = 29 mΩ. A general-purpose 100 µF electrolytic usually has more, so use a low-ESR part or a ceramic.

quiz.q: Find the skin depth in copper at 100 kHz and state the strand thickness you would use.
quiz.a: δ = √(ρ/(π f µ<sub>0</sub>)) = √(1.72 × 10<sup>−8</sup>/(π × 10⁵ × 4π × 10<sup>−7</sup>)) ≈ 0.21 mm, where ρ is copper resistivity. Use strands under about twice this, that is under 0.4 mm, or litz wire.

quiz.q: Why does the window area limit a transformer design?
quiz.a: Copper for both windings must fit in the window with a fill factor of about 0.4, so N<sub>p</sub>A<sub>p</sub> + N<sub>s</sub>A<sub>s</sub> ≤ k<sub>u</sub>A<sub>w</sub>. If it does not fit, a larger core is needed, otherwise the wire is too thin and the winding overheats.

quiz.q: A flyback transformer is built on an ungapped ferrite core. Explain what fails.
quiz.a: Without a gap the core reluctance R<sub>c</sub> is small, so saturation current I<sub>sat</sub> = B<sub>max</sub>·A<sub>e</sub>·R<sub>c</sub>/N is only a fraction of an amp. Primary current reaches it before the end of the on-time, inductance collapses, and current then rises limited only by leakage inductance, giving a large spike and switch failure.

beyond: Not for the exam. Industry uses the area-product method to pick a core in one step: compare A<sub>e</sub>·A<sub>w</sub> with the value the design needs. Planar magnetics, with windings etched on a PCB, and litz wire are standard above 100 kHz. Wide band-gap devices push switching to hundreds of kilohertz, which shrinks L and C but makes core loss and AC resistance the limiting factors.
